abstract.p: Policy discontinuities complicate investment in electric two-wheeler (E2W) manufacturing, battery services and charging infrastructure. This study developed a lifecycle-cost and diffusion framework to support engineering-management decisions in Indonesia. Six annual observations from the type-approval registration certificate (SRUT, Sertifikat Registrasi Uji Tipe) system, covering 2020–2025, were combined with motorcycle distribution data and a distance-dependent total cost of ownership (TCO) model. Discounted cost differences between internal combustion engine (ICE) motorcycles and E2Ws were converted into bounded economic attractiveness and coupled separately to Logistic, Gompertz and Bass specifications. The private-use case assumed 15,000 km/year over eight years, while a 40,000 km/year swapping-service case examined battery-risk allocation and tariff exposure. SRUT increments declined from 77,078 in 2024 to 59,232 in 2025, a 23.2% reduction. The private-use discounted cost advantage fell from Rp14.79 million to Rp8.10 million over the same years. The in-sample root mean square errors were 5,788, 5,998 and 9,015 annual units for Gompertz-economic, Logistic-economic and Bass-economic, respectively. Across five policy scenarios, their 2040 annual adoption ranges were 0.814–0.974, 1.563–1.859 and 1.934–3.670 million units. At the private-use energy intensity, these ranges implied 0.427–1.927 TWh of full-year traction energy for the new 2040 cohort. Calibration-window sensitivity was substantial, so the ranges describe conditional planning cases rather than validated forecasts. The framework connects vehicle economics with staged capacity decisions while distinguishing rider affordability from service-system requirements.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: The transition to electric two-wheelers (E2Ws) creates a coordination problem for engineering managers. Vehicle production, battery procurement, charging access and aftersales capacity must expand on different investment cycles, while demand responds to purchase assistance, fuel prices and confidence in battery services. Expanding these systems too early can leave costly assets underused; expanding them too late can restrict vehicle uptake and service reliability. A useful planning model must therefore connect adopter economics with a range of demand conditions and identify which operational quantities still require local measurement.

Indonesia illustrates this problem. Annual E2W increments reported from Ministry of Transportation type-approval registration certificate (SRUT, Sertifikat Registrasi Uji Tipe) records rose from 2,109 units in 2020 to 77,078 in 2024, then fell to a retrospectively reported 59,232 in 2025 [1]. The 23.2% decline coincided with a change in purchase-assistance conditions; the aggregate series alone cannot identify its cause. The 2025 ratio of SRUT increments to Indonesian Motorcycle Industry Association (AISI) domestic motorcycle distribution was 0.924% (59,232/6,412,769) [2]. This combines different administrative measures and is an indicative penetration ratio rather than a precisely matched retail market share. Information System for Purchase Assistance of Two-Wheeled Battery Electric Vehicles (SISAPIRa) assistance counts [3] and industrial-roadmap targets [4] are treated separately from observed registrations.

Innovation diffusion theory and the Bass model provide interpretable descriptions of adoption over time [5], [6]. Generalised formulations incorporate decision variables [7], and comparisons of electric vehicle (EV) diffusion models show why curve choice matters for long-range results [8]. Bitencourt et al. [9] introduced an economic-attractiveness adjustment into a policy-sensitive Bass application. More recently, Domarchi and Cherchi [10] reviewed the integration of choice behaviour, diffusion and substitution, while Li et al. [11] explicitly connected total cost of ownership (TCO), a green premium and generalised Bass forecasting. Accordingly, linking TCO to diffusion is established prior work. The present study addresses the narrower task of applying a common discounted cost signal to three alternative specifications while separating private battery ownership from high-utilisation swapping services.

The framework compares discounted internal combustion engine (ICE) and E2W ownership costs, converts their difference into a bounded economic-response term and evaluates adoption under five policy scenarios. The cost assumptions are shared across the three diffusion specifications, so differences in their outputs can be traced to their temporal structure and fitted coefficients. Applying the workflow elsewhere requires local inputs and re-estimation.

sec.title: 1.1. Research questions
sec.p: Three research questions connect the economic module to system planning:
RQ1. How do mileage, maintenance, battery replacement, residual value and energy-service tariffs determine the discounted cost advantage of E2W ownership?
RQ2. How do three economically adjusted diffusion specifications differ when calibrated to the same short registration series and used under a common scenario protocol?
RQ3. What do the resulting adoption ranges imply for energy demand, battery services and staged infrastructure decisions, and which conclusions depend on unobserved operational inputs?

sec.title: 1.2. Contributions
sec.p: The study combines distance-dependent battery replacement accounting with a comparison of three economically adjusted diffusion specifications. It then converts annual adoption scenarios into full-year traction-energy requirements for newly added vehicles. Private battery ownership and high-utilisation service contracts have separate cost boundaries. Policy cases retain the coefficients fitted to the baseline data, allowing changed cost inputs to be followed through each specification. Table 1 summarises these planning applications.

sec.title: 2.1. Diffusion models and the adoption measure
sec.p: Innovation diffusion theory describes how adoption develops through communication, perceived relative advantage and social influence [5]. Bass [6] formalised external influence and imitation in a model for durable goods. Reviews of innovation diffusion [12], [13] show that parameter interpretation depends on the market boundary and the adoption measure. These foundations remain relevant, but a model of first adoption in a fixed population cannot be transferred without qualification to annual motorcycle registrations in a changing replacement market.

Logistic and Gompertz curves offer symmetric and asymmetric transition shapes. Scorrano and Danielis [14] modelled Italian electric two-wheeler uptake using an agent-based specification parameterised from a discrete choice experiment. Comparative EV work [8], [15] and the review by Domarchi and Cherchi [10] show how behavioural representation and forecast evaluation differ across modelling families. Here, Logistic and Gompertz levels multiply annual market ceilings, whereas Bass generates a recursive adoption flow. Comparing these constructions shows how the temporal specification affects planning results.

sec.title: 2.2. Economic adjustments to diffusion
sec.p: Generalised Bass models allow prices and other decision variables to modify diffusion [7]. For policy analysis, an economic channel is easier to audit than an undifferentiated policy dummy: a purchase subsidy changes acquisition expenditure, a fuel-price assumption changes ICE operating expenditure, and an energy-service tariff changes E2W operating expenditure. Converting these changes into a common discounted cost difference makes their accounting effects comparable, although it does not estimate how consumers causally respond to each instrument.

Bitencourt et al. [9] used payback-based economic attractiveness in a policy-sensitive Bass model, and Li et al. [11] linked a TCO-based green premium to generalised Bass forecasting. Building on this economic channel, the present study applies a common lifecycle-cost boundary to three diffusion specifications and distinguishes battery ownership from recurring service payments. Its response slopes are fitted to aggregate registrations; the threshold is an explicit planning assumption.

sec.title: 2.3. Lifecycle cost and replacement economics
sec.p: TCO analysis compares acquisition expenditure with discounted energy, maintenance and resale costs [16]. For Indonesian electric motorcycles, Fathoni et al. [17] considered how refurbishment, second-life use and recycling alter battery-related costs. Cross-country TCO analysis also links ownership economics to market uptake [18]. Incentive research [19], green-premium policy modelling [20] and Indonesian system-dynamics analysis [21] place these costs within wider adoption decisions. ASEAN comparisons [22], Vietnamese E2W analysis [23] and the EV TCO review [24] further show why vehicle class, ownership horizon and service arrangements must be specified before cost results are compared.

Mileage affects both sides of the E2W comparison. Greater use increases avoided fuel expenditure but also brings battery replacement forward and can reduce resale value. Chien et al. [25] showed how battery swapping shifts battery expenditure from acquisition to recurring payments in Taiwan. Gurusamy et al. [26] compared E2Ws using vehicle performance and driving-cycle criteria. Together, these studies support specifying the vehicle and service arrangement before comparing ownership costs. The present model includes distance-based energy and maintenance expenditure, discrete replacement events and a mileage adjustment to residual value.

sec.title: 2.4. Indonesian context and service contracts
sec.p: Indonesian studies have examined E2W cost competitiveness [27], adoption determinants and changes in travel behaviour [28], and interactions between policy and lifecycle costs [21]. Asian Development Bank roadmap [29] addresses charging and swapping infrastructure. Purchase-assistance regulations [30], [31], the industrial roadmap [4] and SISAPIRa [3] establish the policy and programme context. Registration observations, policy provisions and cost assumptions are kept distinct in the analysis.

The compiled sources do not provide national weights for private, logistics and ride-hailing users. The analysis therefore retains a 15,000 km/year private-use calibration case and a separate 40,000 km/year high-utilisation stress test. Setiawan et al. [32] examined Indonesian swapping-industry policy through system dynamics; al Irsyad et al. [33] compared commercial-vehicle and motorcycle-conversion costs in ASEAN. Both are relevant to distinguishing service-provider decisions from rider costs. Here, Rp7,750/kWh is an assumed service tariff close to rider cost parity in the baseline case, not a measured national price. It includes an allowance for battery availability, so future replacement is not also charged directly to the rider.

sec.title: 2.5. Research gap and analytical boundary
sec.p: This study addresses a planning task that lies between detailed behavioural modelling and aggregate cost comparison. Existing work links economics to diffusion [9], [11], evaluates E2W ownership costs [22], [23], [27] and represents infrastructure feedback [21], [32]. The present comparison uses one cost-accounting structure across alternative temporal specifications, then carries their differences into resource requirements. This design makes the influence of model choice visible when consistent national observations are sparse.

Evidence from Vietnam [34] and India [35] identifies price, range, charging access, charging time and battery-related concerns as adoption factors. Operational studies examine travel-chain-based swapping demand [36], service pricing [37] and network deployment under driver range anxiety and impatience [38]. These findings motivate the separation of national annual adoption from local service-system design: station queues and spatial coverage require operational data beyond an annual registration series.

The accounting module determines whether E2W ownership has a discounted cost advantage; the diffusion specifications determine how that signal enters annual adoption. Operating savings can preserve an advantage after purchase assistance ends, whereas a high service tariff can offset those savings. The scenario comparison examines both effects without assuming that a given cost difference uniquely determines consumer uptake.

Annual adoption scenarios provide the first input to engineering planning. New additions determine cohort energy requirements; active stock and local utilisation determine charging, swapping and aftersales demand. This study quantifies the first link and identifies the further operating coefficients needed for capacity decisions.

sec.title: 3.1. Data and analytical design
sec.p: Calibration uses six annual SRUT E2W increments for 2020–2025 and AISI domestic motorcycle distribution as the market-scale series (Table 3). SRUT increments are an administrative adoption proxy, while the AISI denominator measures domestic distribution. Their ratio is therefore indicative rather than a matched retail share. Forward total-market values are exogenous inputs. The model separates this market-scale assumption from the fitted economic-response and temporal coefficients.

The private-use case covers 15,000 km/year over eight years. The 8% real discount rate, 4% annual decline in the purchase-cohort battery benchmark, and ICE/E2W residual fractions of 45%/20% are planning assumptions. The high-utilisation case covers 40,000 km/year under an effective service tariff that includes battery availability. Within each purchase cohort, selected fuel prices and recurring operating costs are held constant in real terms. This convention supports comparable policy cases rather than reconstructing realised household expenditure.

sec.p: The Logistic and Gompertz inflection indices (24.6827 and 33.4675) both lie outside the 2020–2040 analysis window. They are fitted shape parameters rather than reliable estimates of market take-off. Reported coefficients are rounded; reproducing precise fit statistics requires the unrounded calibration outputs.

The three specifications were fitted separately by nonlinear least squares. Table 5 reports rounded coefficients. Exact reproduction of the optimisation requires parameter bounds, starting values, stopping tolerances and unrounded estimates, together with the annual market inputs. These numerical calibration records are not included in the present manuscript. Appendix D checks historical Logistic and Gompertz predictions by substituting the displayed inputs and rounded coefficients; this is an arithmetic consistency check rather than an independent refit.

The calibration-window assessment comprises six leave-one-year-out fits and three paired deletions: 2020–2021, 2023–2024, and 2020 with 2025. These nine specified cases examine dependence on observations and policy-period coverage. The full six-year fit remains the baseline, retaining the 2025 reversal. Section 5.1 reports the resulting changes.

sec.title: 3.6. Country-specific recalibration
sec.p: Application in another country requires local sales, prices, tariffs, mileage, battery life, residual values and policy inputs. The discounted cost difference must then be recomputed and the diffusion coefficients re-estimated against a consistently defined local adoption series. The Indonesian coefficients describe this calibration and should not be treated as behavioural constants across markets.

Country-specific application requires a consistent definition of the adoption target before transferring any equations. Vietnam would require local E2W category boundaries and charging-access inputs [23], [34]; India would require local price, range, charging-time and network information [35]. The same principle applies elsewhere. These examples identify data requirements rather than provide second-country results.

Table 6 sets out this recalibration procedure; Appendix A identifies the corresponding workbook sheets. Without national segment weights, the commercial-use calculation remains a separate stress test.

sec.title: 4.1. Historical lifecycle economics
sec.p: The modelled private-use cost advantage increased from Rp1.95 million for the 2020 cohort to Rp14.79 million for the 2024 cohort, then fell to Rp8.10 million for the 2025 cohort (Table 3). Two battery replacements occur within each eight-year private-use horizon. The change reflects the combined accounting effects of purchase assistance, fuel-price assumptions, battery benchmarks and discounted residual proceeds. Its direction agrees with the registration reversal, although the aggregate series cannot separate these influences from concurrent market changes.

sec.title: 4.2. Retrospective fit comparison
sec.p: The in-sample fit statistics are compared in Table 7.
The in-sample RMSE values are compared in Figure 4.

caption.title: Reported in-sample errors for the four specifications

sec.p: Gompertz-economic and Logistic-economic have in-sample RMSEs of 5,788 and 5,998 annual units, respectively. Their difference is about 3.5% of the Logistic error and does not establish a meaningful forecasting advantage in this six-year sample. Bass-economic records 9,015 units and pure Bass 16,766 units. Substitution of the displayed inputs and rounded coefficients reproduces the first two RMSEs to within one annual unit (Appendix D). The economic adjustment adds a fitted coefficient relative to pure Bass, so the lower training errors alone do not demonstrate better predictive performance. Percentage errors are also sensitive to the small early-period observations.

sec.p: The 2040 planning envelopes across the five scenarios are compared in Figure 5.

caption.title: Reported 2040 adoption potential across five policy scenarios

sec.p: Across S0–S4, 2040 annual adoption ranges from 0.814 to 0.974 million for Gompertz-economic, 1.563 to 1.859 million for Logistic-economic and 1.934 to 3.670 million for Bass-economic. In S0, Bass is approximately 2.38 times Gompertz, a difference of 1.120 million annual additions. The substantial spread across specifications motivates testing several demand cases before selecting a capacity commitment.

Relative to S0, Rp7 million assistance increases 2040 adoption by approximately 15.5% for Logistic, 15.9% for Gompertz and 75.0% for Bass. Raising fuel from Rp15,000 to Rp20,000/litre adds only 0.027 million units in Logistic and 0.016 million in Gompertz. The sigmoid approaches saturation as the cost advantage rises. Bass responds more strongly because an earlier increase also affects subsequent imitation through the cumulative recursion.

sec.p: The private-use and high-utilisation cost sensitivities are compared in Table 9.

sec.p: The high-utilisation case has six distance-triggered battery-life intervals ending before year eight, compared with two in the private case. These are technical replacement equivalents under the assumed 50,000 km battery life, not six observed swapping transactions. At Rp7,750/kWh and fuel at Rp10,000/litre, the reported rider cost advantage is only Rp0.54 million and Logistic-economic attractiveness is 0.241. Higher fuel-price scenarios raise the cost difference to Rp26.08 million and Rp51.62 million. The results depend on the service contract: battery availability is included in the tariff, so adding separate replacement expenditure would count the same provision twice.

The small discounted advantage in the base service case indicates that rider cost competitiveness is sensitive to the assumed tariff. This result concerns rider expenditure under the specified contract; it does not establish service-provider profitability. National adoption implications also depend on the proportions of private and commercial users.

sec.title: 5.1. Calibration sensitivity and identification
sec.p: Each economically adjusted specification fits three coefficients to six observations. With the response threshold, cost assumptions and market scale fixed, economic response and temporal growth can partly compensate for one another. Small in-sample errors therefore provide limited evidence about parameter identification or performance beyond 2025. Deletion diagnostics assess dependence on the selected years, while differences between specifications indicate structural sensitivity; neither yields a statistical prediction interval.

Relative deletion changes are calculated by subtracting the full-sample estimate from the subset estimate, dividing by the full-sample estimate and multiplying by 100. The same convention applies to output changes. Deleting observations is useful for locating influential periods, but a fit evaluated on the retained years is not a forecast test. Results evaluated against all six years likewise remain retrospective diagnostics.

The deletion results show substantial calibration-window dependence. Omitting 2020 changes 2040 S0 adoption by -7.3% for Logistic, -5.1% for Gompertz and -18.0% for Bass. Omitting 2022 reduces the respective outputs by 66.9%, 49.0% and 92.4%. Excluding 2025 raises them to 4.104, 1.599 and 6.579 million units, compared with 1.563, 0.814 and 1.934 million in the full fit. The underlying subset records are mapped to AISI_Robustness in Appendix A. These changes make the post-assistance observation central to the long-range interpretation.

sec.title: 5.2. Saturation of the economic response
sec.p:
For cost advantage expressed in million rupiah, the response derivative is
α A A ( − ) 1
. It becomes small as $A$ approaches one, explaining the narrowing difference between the higher fuel-price cases. Fuel prices continue to change TCO, but their effect on the Logistic and Gompertz annual multipliers diminishes. This behaviour follows from the selected response function.

At that stage, charging access, range and service availability deserve separate operational assessment. The Indonesian roadmap [29] and evidence from Vietnam and India [34], [35] identify these practical concerns. A saturated economic response cannot determine whether a network can deliver the corresponding service volume.

sec.title: 5.3. Battery services and high utilisation
sec.p: High annual distance changes the allocation of costs as well as their magnitude. Under private battery ownership, replacement is a discrete expenditure borne by the rider. Under the specified service contract, it is embedded in recurring payments and becomes an asset-management obligation for the provider. This distinction is consistent with studies of swapping-industry policy [32] and service pricing [37]. The near-parity base case shows why high mileage alone is insufficient to justify fleet conversion at a chosen tariff.

Operational planning requires a further distinction between swapping frequency and battery retirement. A rider may exchange a battery many times before that battery reaches its usable-life limit. The six technical turnover equivalents in this study therefore cannot be used to size daily station throughput. Travel-chain data, usable pack energy, charging turnaround and service availability are needed for that calculation [36], [38]. Platform contracts should also specify responsibility for battery health, service interruptions and tariff changes; these obligations affect feasibility even when vehicle-level discounted cost is favourable.

sec.title: 5.4. Engineering management and resource planning
sec.p: Under the retained calibration, Gompertz gives the lowest 2040 adoption range, Logistic an intermediate range and Bass the highest range. This ordering offers contrasting demand cases for capacity assessment. It is specific to the fitted data and assumptions, rather than a general ranking of the three model families.

Staged investment offers one use of the scenario comparison. Long-lead assets with substantial irrecoverable cost can be assessed under lower demand, expandable capacity under intermediate demand, and procurement options or short-lead additions under upper demand. Selecting a preferred plan additionally requires investment costs, lead times, utilisation targets and service-level constraints.

The resource-planning implications in Table 10 can be quantified for traction energy. At the assumed annual distance and energy intensity, each private-use E2W requires 15,000 × 0.035 = 525 kWh per year. Multiplying this value by the modelled annual additions in 2040 gives the full-year energy requirements for the new cohort in Table 11. These are full-year requirements for the newly added cohort, not national 2040 electricity consumption: vehicles enter throughout the year, earlier cohorts remain in use, and charging losses and commercial mileage are excluded. Total fleet energy additionally requires active stock and retirement assumptions. Station counts further require spatial demand, usable throughput and a service-level target; battery inventory requires charging turnaround, failure rates and safety stock. The separation prevents annual additions from being mistaken for the active fleet.
The principal engineering-management interpretations are summarised in Table 10.

sec.title: 5.5. Policy interpretation
sec.p: The policy comparison traces cost channels. Assistance reduces acquisition expenditure, while higher fuel prices raise the ICE operating-cost benchmark. Bass amplifies earlier changes through cumulative imitation. These mechanisms explain differences within the model; causal evaluation would require a design that separates policy changes from other market developments.

For private riders with an existing lifecycle-cost advantage, further assistance has a diminishing effect within the bounded response. High-utilisation riders remain sensitive to service tariffs and the allocation of battery risk. Policy assessment should therefore pair affordability analysis with service feasibility, adding household, provider and fiscal data when evaluating a complete support package.

sec.title: 5.6. Assumption and scenario sensitivity
sec.p: Table 12 and Table 13 distinguish recalibration sensitivity from fixed-coefficient scenario sensitivity. In Table 12, changing historical TCO assumptions and refitting the models alters both economics and curve shape. For example, an E2W residual fraction of 10% gives Bass-economic 1.610 million annual units in 2040, while 35% gives 2.958 million, against 1.934 million in the base case. Logistic and Gompertz can move non-monotonically because coefficient re-estimation offsets part of the direct cost effect. These outputs are not pure marginal effects of the changed input.

Table 13 instead keeps fitted coefficients fixed. Its first two cases change the annual cap while retaining the baseline Bass planning pool M; they therefore test cap scaling, not complete redefinition of the Bass eligible market. The tariff cases affect only the high-utilisation cost comparison. Keeping these experiments separate makes their interpretation clearer, but neither experiment supplies a probability distribution for future adoption.

The sensitivity outputs in Table 12 and Table 13 were obtained from the companion workbook’s Sensitivity_DataTable sheet. Unless stated otherwise, adoption values refer to the 2040 no-new-policy case. Table 12 refits coefficients after changing historical TCO assumptions; Table 13 retains coefficients. In the annual-cap cases, the baseline Bass planning pool M remains fixed. Rounding may affect the last reported digit.

sec.title: 5.7. Transferability and replication
sec.p: The framework transfers as a sequence of operations: define the adoption measure, specify the cost boundary, compute discounted advantage, calibrate alternative trajectories and convert demand cases into resource requirements. Local application must replace the Indonesian inputs and coefficients. A consistent adoption definition is essential before recalibration.

A conventional train-test split would leave very few observations for estimating three coefficients. No independent forecast evaluation is therefore reported. The retrospective fit and deletion diagnostics address different, narrower questions: agreement with the observed series and sensitivity to its composition. When later observations become available, the fitted specifications should be evaluated without using those observations for parameter selection.

Country adaptation requires local vehicle categories, registration or distribution data, prices, tariffs, battery life, maintenance, residual values and policy chronology. Operational conversion additionally needs mileage distributions, charging efficiency, service throughput and retirement information. Segment weights should enter national aggregation only when they can be estimated from observations.

sec.title: 5.8. Limitations and future work
sec.p: The six-year calibration window limits separation of economic response from temporal growth. Deletion results show substantial extrapolation sensitivity, and long-range outputs also depend on the exogenous market path, 75% share ceiling and Bass pool definition. The scenario ranges therefore have no assigned probabilities and do not establish causal policy effects. Exact reproduction of the Bass projections, recalibrated sensitivities and deletion cases additionally requires numerical records beyond the rounded Tables provided here. Those calculations cannot be independently established from endpoint values alone.

The cost module represents one vehicle class with selected operating assumptions. Financing, insurance, taxes and downtime are outside its boundary. Fuel prices remain constant within each cohort, and future battery events use the purchase-cohort benchmark. These conventions simplify comparison but omit variation among households, contracts and battery technologies. More detailed cost boundaries would require consistent recalibration.

Supply, grid connections, spatial charging access, station queues and provider profitability are also outside the diffusion model. The energy conversion establishes an accounting link from additions to resource demand. Monthly or regional registrations, pack-level degradation and station operating records would support a subsequent assessment of system capacity and service performance.

The next empirical test is performance against registrations observed after 2025. A longer series would also allow a more informative assessment of parameter stability. Network feedback or adopter heterogeneity could then be added where independent operating or behavioural data support the additional parameters.

sec.title: 6. Conclusions
sec.p: This study linked distance-dependent lifecycle costs with three economically adjusted adoption specifications for engineering-management planning in Indonesia. Registrations increased through 2024 and declined in 2025; over the latter interval, the modelled private-use cost advantage fell from Rp14.79 million to Rp8.10 million. The cost calculation attributes this modelled change to the selected acquisition-support and operating-cost assumptions, without identifying the cause of the registration decline.

Across the five policy cases, 2040 annual adoption ranged from 0.814 to 0.974 million for Gompertz-economic, 1.563 to 1.859 million for Logistic-economic and 1.934 to 3.670 million for Bass-economic. These are conditional scenario outputs. Similar historical errors for Gompertz and Logistic do not resolve their long-range divergence, and the deletion diagnostics show strong dependence on the calibration period. At 525 kWh per vehicle-year, the corresponding new-cohort traction-energy requirements span 0.427–1.927 TWh for a full operating year.

In the high-utilisation service case, Rp7,750/kWh and Rp10,000/litre yield a discounted rider advantage of only Rp0.54 million. The corresponding cost-parity tariff is approximately Rp7,817/kWh. This narrow margin makes the service contract and allocation of battery risk central to fleet-conversion decisions.

The framework makes the accounting link between rider costs, annual additions and cohort energy requirements explicit. Its practical use is to examine how a capacity commitment performs under different demand assumptions. Investment selection still requires active-fleet estimates, local operating data, service requirements and project costs. Evaluation against subsequent registrations is needed before the adoption trajectories can support stronger forecasting claims.

The fuel-price assumption raises discounted ICE expenditure by Rp4.502 million between the two cohort comparisons. The lower battery benchmark reduces discounted E2W replacement expenditure by Rp1.647 million. Together they raise the discounted E2W cost advantage from Rp1.948 million to Rp8.097 million, giving Logistic-economic attractiveness of 0.313 and 0.689, respectively. This is a decomposition of the model’s accounting channel, not an estimate of the causes of observed registration changes.

This appendix calculates historical private-use costs and Logistic and Gompertz predictions from the inputs in Table 3, Table 4, and Table 5 and Appendix C. The rounded coefficients in Table 5 are substituted without refitting. The exercise checks the arithmetic of the reported specification; it does not test forecast performance or verify the original optimisation.

For each calendar year, annual fuel and maintenance payments are discounted with the factor 5.7466389437. Battery events occur at years 10/3 and 20/3. The event-price benchmark is Rp6.5 million multiplied by 0.96 for each year after 2020, with the same cohort benchmark used at both events. Residual proceeds are discounted over eight years. Assistance is Rp7 million for the 2023 and 2024 cohorts and zero otherwise.

The resulting cost difference in rupiah is converted to million rupiah in Eq. (9). Attractiveness is then multiplied by 0.75, the observed annual AISI distribution and the relevant kernel level. Table D1 reports the reconstructed historical values. Rounding is applied only for presentation.

Using unrounded reconstructed predictions gives RMSE = 5,997.99 annual units for Logistic-economic and 5,788.34 for Gompertz-economic. These round to 5,998 and 5,788, respectively, matching Table 7. Small differences from an implementation using unrounded fitted coefficients are expected.

Reproducing the forward calculations requires annual R2 values through 2040. Bass calculations also require the numerical planning pool M and its consistent use in fitting and projection. Recalibrated sensitivities and deletion diagnostics require the associated optimiser settings and parameter records. These inputs cannot be uniquely recovered from rounded scenario endpoints.

notes.title: Data Availability Statement
notes.p: The annual administrative observations are reproduced in Table 3, with sources listed in References [1], [2], [3], [4], [30], [31]. Table 4 and Table 5 provide cost assumptions and rounded coefficients; Appendices C and D give worked cost calculations and historical Logistic and Gompertz predictions. The model workbook is provided as supplementary material, with its sheet structure summarised in Appendix A. It contains the complete annual market path, the SRUT series and its reconciliation (sheet SRUT_Audit), unrounded coefficients, scenario and sensitivity outputs, and the non-private depreciation inputs. Coefficients were estimated by bounded multi-start nonlinear least squares; the standalone optimisation code and complete optimiser configuration are not included.
